title: Staircases in the Home: Position, Style and Safety for Seniors, Children
desc: Choosing a staircase position and type: straight, L, U, spiral; safety tips for seniors and children such as handrails, railings and lighting.
summary: Pros and cons of staircase types in homes, how to choose a position, and safety details for seniors and young children that homeowners should request in the design.
body: p

The staircase is where the whole family walks many times a day, and also where falls easily happen, especially for seniors and young children. Choosing the right position, type and safety details from the design stage avoids costly repairs later.
h2
1. Choosing the staircase position
ul
In the middle of the house, next to a light well: common in tube houses; the staircase gets natural light and the route to the rooms is short.
Along a side wall: keeps the rest of the floor plan open, suited to a narrow frontage.
Near the exit: convenient for getting out in an emergency. The route from the foot of the stairs to the front door should not be blocked by vehicles or furniture.
p

In a fire, the staircase is often the only escape route from the upper floors. Do not store flammable items under or at the foot of the stairs. See also Fire prevention and fighting requirements for houses.
h2
2. Comparing staircase types
ul
Single straight flight: simple and cheap, but takes up a lot of length, and a fall means sliding a long way.
L-shaped and U-shaped stairs with landings: a landing lets seniors stop to rest and limits tumbling down a whole flight; suited to multi-generational homes.
Stairs with winder treads (triangular steps at corners): save space, but the narrow inner part of the tread easily causes a misstep – best limited if the home has seniors.
Spiral stairs: attractive and compact, but hard to climb and to carry things on – only suitable as a secondary stair to the rooftop or a mezzanine.
Stringer (fishbone) stairs and open-riser steps: airy and modern; pay attention to the gaps between steps so young children's feet cannot slip through.
h2
3. Step dimensions: even and comfortable
p

The most important point is that the steps within the same flight must have equal heights and equal widths. Even a small difference in one step easily makes someone misstep. The step height and width, flight width and headroom are calculated by the architect according to the floor height and the area allotted to the staircase; homeowners should check these carefully on the drawings and avoid letting workers “redivide” the steps on their own during construction.
h2
4. Safety details for seniors and young children
ol
Sturdy handrails that fit the hand, running continuously along the flight; a home with seniors should have handrails on both sides.
Railings that are high enough with small gaps, and without horizontal bars that are easy to climb like steps.
Non-slip step surfaces: avoid polished stone, and wood with glossy coating; non-slip nosing strips can be used on the step edges.
Enough light: lamps at the foot and top of the stairs, with switches at both ends; night lights at step level can be added.
Safety gates at the top and foot of the stairs when the home has young children.
A step-edge color different from the tread color helps people with poor eyesight to see them.
h2
5. When to consider a home elevator?
p

For a house of 4 floors or more, with elderly people or people with mobility difficulty, it is advisable to plan an elevator shaft in the structural design in advance, even if it is not installed right away. Cutting slabs to make a shaft after the house is built is both costly and affects the structure, requiring the engineer to recalculate.
h2
6. Staircases and structure
p

Reinforced concrete, steel or wooden stairs must all be designed and calculated for load. For a house that must hire a design firm (3 floors or more, or with a basement, or a floor area of 250 m² or more, or a height of 12 m or more), the staircase is part of that design file (Clause 2, Article 10 of Decree 207/2026/ND-CP). The homeowner is responsible for organizing construction, supervision and safety in the construction of a detached house (Clause 3, Article 10).
p
